Expanding Chemical Space in the Synthesis of Gold
Bipyramids
Ana Sánchez-Iglesias and Marek Grzelczak*

Gold bipyramids (AuBPs), despite having superior properties compared to
their spectroscopically similar counterparts, gold nanorods, have found
comparatively limited applications. This discrepancy is primarily due to the
lack of protocols to tailor their dimensions. Typically, the concentration of Au
seeds is virtually the sole factor that determines the aspect ratio and thus, the
optical properties of AuBPs. As a result, varying the volumes of AuBPs while
incurring minimal changes to their optical spectra remains a synthetically
non-trivial task. Here, the chemical space in the seeded growth of AuBPs, is
expanded by exploiting the interplay between bromide, silver ions, and seed
concentration for tuning the ﬁnal dimensions and optical properties of AuBPs.
Speciﬁcally, a 6 fold change in volumes of AuBPs is achieved while
maintaining the ﬁxed plasmon band position. Further overgrowth of
as-prepared bipyramids broadens the realizable dimensions without
compromising quality and initial morphology. Overall, the results expand the
chemical toolbox in the wet-chemistry synthesis of anisotropic gold
nanoparticles, which is relevant for health, colorimetric sensors, and energy
applications.
1. Introduction

Gold bipyramids (AuBPs) are gaining signiﬁcant popularity as a
class of anisotropic nanocrystals due to their superior plasmonic
performance compared to gold nanorods.[1,2] Due to low radia-
tive damping, the AuBPs feature exceptional narrow plasmon
linewidth,[3,4] large local electric ﬁeld enhancements at the sharp
tips,[5,6] rendering them an appealing platform for sensors,[7–12]

imaging devices,[13,14] coupled[15,16] and nonlinear[17] hybrid sys-
tems. The penta-twinned crystalline structure improves the

The application rate of AuBPs in various
ﬁelds goes hand in hand with the progress
in synthetic methods for their preparation.
Over the last two decades, we witnessed
major breakthroughs in the synthesis of
gold bipyramids involving i) the need
for pentatwinned seeds to render bipyra-
mid morphology,[29] ii) reversible silver
overgrowth to increase nanocrystals yield
through
post-synthetic
puriﬁcation,[7,30]

iii) the use of hydroxyquinoline as an
alternative
reducing
agent,[31]
iv)
ther-
mal treatment of seeds[31,32] to increase
the yield (85%) without the need for
post-synthetic puriﬁcation.[32] These pro-
tocols remain highly constrained, that
is, controlling the volume while keeping
a constant aspect ratio is synthetically
challenging, a feature that is central for modulating scattering-
to-extinction ratio,[33] which, on the other hand, determines the
targeted applications.[34] Thus, there is an urgent need for ex-
panding the chemical space in the synthesis of gold bipyramids
to unlock their dimensional and optical diversity, as has been
also indicated by data-driven analysis of protocols available in the
literature.[35,36]

The chemical space of gold bipyramids encompasses six key
parameters: surfactant, gold precursor, silver ions, reducing
agent, pH, and seeds, with the seed concentration playing a
pivotal role in determining the aspect ratio. Nevertheless, ad-
justing the seed concentration simultaneously impacts the ﬁnal
nanocrystal volume, complicating systematic investigations into
volume-dependent plasmonic properties, such as photo-thermal
conversion and[37,38] plasmon-exciton coupling.[15,16] Parola and
co-workers[31] have attempted to address this challenge by ex-
amining the inﬂuence of surfactant counterions on the as-
pect ratio of bipyramids. Their ﬁndings revealed that bromide
(Br−) in cetyltrimethylammonium (CTA+) leads to nanocrys-
tals with low aspect ratios, whereas a mixture of bromide
and chloride (Br−/Cl−) in CTA+ promotes the formation of
elongated bipyramids, termed nanojavelins. Furthermore, the
same group demonstrated that varying CTAB concentrations
in a single-surfactant system can suppress the production of
isotropic nanoparticles.[39] These results suggest that the role of

counterion interactions within surfactant systems could serve as
an additional parameter in controlling the dimensions of gold
bipyramids. However, the practical implementation of this ap-
proach remains a challenge.

This work deals with expanding the structural parameters of
AuBPs through ﬁne-tuning of synthetic parameters. The main
ﬁnding is that CTAB as an additive (being CTAC the primary sur-
factant), can tailor the aspect ratio of AuBPs at ﬁxed volume. This
is in stark contrast to the state-of-the-art, where similar modula-
tions of localized surface plasmon resonance (LSPR) maxima re-
quired varying the amount of Au seeds, and ultimately changing
the volumes of ﬁnal AuBPs.[32] Kinetic studies showed that the
bipyramidal morphology is favored under a fast reduction rate
(low CTAB concentration), indicating that the growth pathway of
AuBPs is a subtle interplay between kinetic control and surface
passivation. Accordingly, we showed that silver nitrate, although
critical for symmetry breaking, has a minor eﬀect on tailoring
the aspect ratio of ﬁnal bipyramids. Furthermore, we found that
by ﬁne-tuning seeds and CTAB concentrations, one can obtain
AuBPs of similar plasmon band position (e.g., 750 nm) and a 6
fold change in volume. The overgrowth of the as-prepared bipyra-
mids allows for expanding available dimensions while conserv-
ing the original shape.
2. Results and Discussion

This work builds on the previous ﬁndings in which Bromide
(Br−) ions induce symmetry breaking to render anisotropic
nanoparticles (nanorods) in the presence of hexadecyltrimethy-
lammonium chloride (CTAC) as the primary surfactant,[40,41]

where Br−ions are responsible for preferential adsorption of
CTA+ molecules on high-energy gold facets[42–45] and alter the
reduction potential of gold ions,[46] favoring thus anisotropic
growth. We hypothesized that by modulating CTAB while keep-
ing the concentration of CTAC as the primary surfactant con-
stant, one could modulate the reduction rate of gold precursor
and, thus, the aspect ratio of AuBPs. To evaluate the hypothesis,
we implemented a standard seeded-growth model that involves
the use of CTAC-stabilized and thermally-aged seed nanocrys-
tals of 6 nm (Videos S1 and S2, Supporting Information)[32] that
are added to the growth solution comprising the cationic surfac-
tants (CTAC and CTAB), silver nitrate, and 8-hydroxyquinoline
(8-HQL) as mild reducing agent at 35 °C. Note that the use of 8-
HQL, instead of ascorbic acid, does not require an extra HCl in
the growth solution to minimize the formation of isotropic by-
product.[31] We found that the synthesis in pure CTAB (100 mM)
renders rice-like bipyramids, while in pure CTAC (100 mM),
bipyramids and isotropic byproducts (Figure 1b; Figure S1, Sup-
porting Information). To evaluate the eﬀect of Br−concentra-
tion on AuBP aspect ratio, we synthesized 13 samples by keep-
ing constant CTAC concentration (100 mM) while modulating
CTAB concentration from 1 to 50 mM, keeping all other ex-
perimental parameters constant (Table S1 and Videos S3 and
S4, Supporting Information). We observed that with increasing
CTAB concentration, the plasmon band position blueshifts from
1070 nm (1 mM CTAB) to 584 nm (50 mM CTAB) (Figure 1c,i).
Accordingly, the structural analysis by transmission electron
microscopy (TEM) conﬁrmed a decrease in length from 100
± 3 nm to 49 ± 4 nm, an increase in width from 17 ± 1 to 29

± 1 nm, and thus decreasing the aspect ratio from 5.9 ± 0.4
to 1.7 ± 0.2 with the increase of CTAB concentration from 1 to
50 mM (Figure 1a,f,h; Figures S2 and S3 and Table S1, Support-
ing Information). Importantly, keeping constant the seeds num-
ber, we could obtain AuBPs of the volume falling in a narrow
range of ≈11 000 nm3 (Figure 1g). The critical role of bromide
ions in the modulation of aspect ratio was conﬁrmed by using
pure KBr instead of CTAB (Figure S4 and Table S2, Supporting
Information), where LSPR blueshifts with increasing bromide
concentration.

It is commonly agreed that the slower the reduction ki-
netics, the larger the shape anisotropy, especially for gold
nanorods.[40,47–49] Intuitively, one expects to obtain AuBPs of a
higher aspect ratio by slowing the reduction kinetics. We per-
formed kinetic studies for all 13 samples in Figure 1 ([CTAB] =
1 – 50 mM) in the presence of CTAC (100 mM), and Au+3:Au0

= 67 molar ratio (Figure 1d,e; Figure S5, Supporting Informa-
tion). At the lowest CTAB concentration (1mM), the gold salt re-
duction was completed in ≈30 min, whereas at 50 mM CTAB,
it required 350 min (Figure 1d,e). With increasing Br−ions
(slowing kinetics), the maximum of the LSPR plasmon band
decreased from 1030 to 584 nm (Figure 1e): the faster the re-
duction, the larger the aspect ratio, indicating that the growth
mechanism of pentatwinned bipyramids is inherently diﬀerent
from that of single crystal gold nanorods[50] and involves an in-
terplay of both kinetic and surface passivation eﬀects.[51] Re-
cent studies show that the growth of bipyramids commences
from pentatwinned seeds to nanograins to receive a bipyrami-
dal shape.[29,39,52] The binding aﬃnity of CTAB to the gold sur-
face is greater than that of CTAC in the presence of silver ions
through the formation of CTA+/[AgBr2]−that exhibit stronger
binding aﬃnity to high index facets as compared to chloride-
bearing CTA+/[AgCl2]−.[52] At the early stage of the growth, the
formed nanograins feature {112} facets[39] that are stabilized pref-
erentially by CTA+/[AgBr2]−. Thus, at high CTAB concentration,
the strong binding of CTA+/[AgBr2]−slows the rate of monomer
feeding (slow kinetics) along the twin axis, rendering low aspect
ratio bipyramids with larger tip curvature (Figure S3, Supporting
Information). At low CTAB concentration, the rate of monomer
feeding is high (fast kinetics) since fewer CTA+/[AgBr2]−are
available to passivate nanograins {112} facets, resulting in a fast
reduction rate along twin axis to render higher aspect ratio bipyra-
mids with sharp tips (Figure S3, Supporting Information).[53]

Additionally, independent of surface events, the variable con-
centration of Br−can alter the ability of gold ions to be re-
duced by 8-HQL because of the diﬀerence in reduction poten-
tial of AuCl2 (1.154 V) and AuBr2 (0.960 V) (Figure S6, Sup-
porting Information).[51] Therefore, the lower the Br−concen-
tration (lower reduction potential), the faster the kinetics, lead-
ing to preferential growth along the long axis. Overall, we pos-
tulate that the growth kinetics of AuBPs resemble the growth
mechanism of gold nanostars, featuring a fast metal deposi-
tion to render spikes, a characteristic property of pentatwinned
nanocrystals.[54–56]

The concentration of Ag+ is a primary parameter in con-
trolling aspect ratio in single-crystalline gold nanorods.[49,57]

We observed that such a principle does not hold for AuBPs.
We performed experiments increasing silver concentration
from 0 to 100 μM while keeping other parameters constant

To expand the synthetic space, we explored the eﬀect of seed
concentration on the dimension of AuBPs at the constant CTAB
concentration (5 mM) (Table S4, Supporting Information). With
increasing seed concentration from 2.5 to 25 μM, the LSPR
blueshifted from 976 to 635 nm (Figure 3d). Accordingly, the
length, width, and volume of the particles progressively de-
creased with increasing seed concentration as the number of
nanoparticles in the growth solution increased (Figure 3a,b,c;
Table S4 and Figure S8, Supporting Information). Importantly,
for the highest seed concentration (25 μM), the dimensions of
AuBPs were substantially reduced to 32 ± 2 by 14 ± 1 nm (volume
≈2300 nm3), being, to our knowledge, the smallest bipyramids
with yield reaching 90% synthesized to date. Note that plasmonic
nanocrystals of reduced volume are of interest for therapeutic
applications, particularly optical hyperthermia[58] or optoacous-
tic imaging[59,60] requiring a high ratio of absorption-to-extinction
cross-section. Since AuBPs exhibit superior thermal stability,[21]

the “minibipyramids” presented here with narrow linewidth are
suitable for the mentioned applications and thus outperform
gold nanorods.[58] Finally, we evaluated the possibility of tailor-
ing the aspect ratio in AuBPs through CTAB concentration for
the Au+3/Au0 molar ratio increasing from 30 to 50 to 67. We ob-
served that regardless of the Au+3/Au0 used, the LSPR redshifted
with decreasing CTAB concentration (Figure 3e; Tables S5 and S6

and Figures S9 and S10, Supporting Information). These results
show that the reasonable combination of CTAB and seed con-
centrations is a convenient tool for controlling the dimensions of
bipyramids.

Typically, an overgrowth of anisotropic nanocrystals (e.g., rods)
leads to the loss of shape anisotropy due to the preferential metal
reduction on high-index facets, rendering isotropic structures of
low-index facets.[61] On the contrary, the particular structure of
bipyramid renders a wide variety of anisotropic morphologies
through the overgrowth.[30] We evaluated the eﬀect of CTAB on
the overgrowth of as-prepared AuBPs (66 and 19 nm, Figure S11,
Supporting Information) without altering the composition of the
growth solution. The concentration of CTAB was increased from
2 to 50 mM while keeping constant the molar ratio of Au+3/Au0 =
5, CTAC = 100 mM, and Ag+ = 30 μM (Table S7, Supporting In-
formation). We observed that upon overgrowth, the initial bipyra-
midal shape was conserved (Figure 4a; Figure S12, Supporting
Information). Similar to the seeded growth from 6 nm spheres,
the concentration of CTAB signiﬁcantly impacted the ﬁnal di-
mensions of AuBPs. Upon the increase of CTAB concentration
(2–50 mM), the length decreased from 173 ± 4 to 76 ± 1 nm
while the width increased from 27 ± 2 to 36 ± 1 nm. The as-
pect ratio decreased from 6.4 to 2.2 (Figure 4b,d). The position
of LSPR of ﬁnal nanoparticles covered the spectral range from
662 to 1274 nm for the limiting CTAB concentrations of 50 and
2 mM, respectively (Figure 4c). Interestingly, at the lowest CTAB

The results presented above indicate that the two experimental
parameters – CTAB and seed concentration – suﬃce to tune the
dimensions broadly and, thus, the optical properties of AuBPs.
We synthesized AuBPs of ﬁxed LSPR at ≈750 nm to demonstrate
such a possibility while varying nanoparticle volume. The seed
concentration was used to vary the volume of ﬁnal nanoparticles
(primary experimental parameter). The concentration of CTAB
was used to ﬁne-tune the position of LSPR at the desired wave-
length (secondary experimental parameter). By executing a se-
quence of experiments, we obtained six samples featuring vir-
tually the same optical properties (Figure 5c), varying their vol-
ume from 3110 to 19702 nm3 (Figure 5a,b). The 6-fold change

of volume at ﬁxed LSPR decreases the scattering-to-extinction
ratio, making the particles relevant for photo-thermal applica-
tions. Note that tailoring volume by seeds and CTAB is valid
for the entire spectral range (Figure S13, Supporting Informa-
tion). Finally, the execution of the study presented here gener-
ated 56 high-quality samples. Figure 5d shows the relationship
of structural and optical properties (length, width, and position
of LSPR) in all samples, where the dimensions of ﬁnal AuBPs
obtained by seeded growth from 6 nm seeds can be substantially
expanded by the overgrowth of as-prepared bipyramids. The po-
sition of LSPR can be tuned from 600 to ≈1300 nm. These re-
sults indicate the possibility for further expansion of available
dimensions.

To quantify the quality presented here AuBPs, we determined
the refractive index sensitivity (RIS) and the Figure of Merit
(FOM)[3,63] for nanocrystals of increasing volume at constant
LSPR (≈800 nm) in water–glycerol mixtures (0–100% in glyc-
erol, Figure S14, Supporting Information).[64] We observed that
increasing particle volume from 3181 to 11160 nm3 increases the
FOM value from 5.2 to 6.3 because of the drop of FWHM and the
increase of RIS with increasing volume of nanoparticles (Figures
S15–S17, Supporting Information). Notably, the obtained FOM
values are the highest reported for this volume range,[65] conﬁrm-
ing nanocrystals of reasonable quality and excellent candidates
for biosensing.

It is widely acknowledged that tip curvature is a key factor in-
ﬂuencing the position of the plasmon in AuBPs.[5,66–68] Even a
slight increase in tip radius by a few nm can cause a signiﬁcant
blueshift in the plasmon band. The rounding of tips can aﬀect
the long-term stability of the LSRP position, potentially compro-
mising targeted applications.[69] We found that the structural in-
tegrity of as-prepared AuBPs is highly dependent on the type of
surfactant used for storage. We monitored the optical properties
of as-prepared AuBPs (LSPR = 900 nm) dispersed in pure CTAC
(10 mM) and pure CTAB (10 mM), and we found that after 30 days
of storage at 27 °C, the maximum of LSPR blueshifted by 45 nm
in CTAB while remained unchanged in CTAC (Figure S18, Sup-
porting Information). A detailed structural analysis of both sam-
ples showed a diﬀerence (0.7 nm) in tip curvature and unaltered
aspect ratio (Figure S18e, Supporting Information). This change
is likely due to the diﬀerence in redox potential between AuBr2
and AuCl2
−, leading to the reshaping of the nanoparticles.[70]

Overall, CTAC is a preferred stabilizer for long-term storage of
AuBPs, as long as the conservation of the initial optical proper-
ties is concerned.
3. Conclusion

We have shown that bromide as a counterion of cationic surfac-
tant is a versatile parameter determining the structural and op-
tical properties of AuBPs. We found an optimal range of CTAB
concentration (1–50 mM), allowing for tailoring the position of

the LSPR across a broad spectral range (600–1300 nm). The in-
crease of bromide in the growth solution slows the kinetics of
precursor reduction and thus inhibits longitudinal growth, giv-
ing rise to a lower aspect ratio. We also found that the concen-
tration of seeds, either thermally-aged spherical nanoparticles or
bipyramids, are additional experimental parameters to tailor the
ﬁnal dimensions of AuBPs. The combination of CTAB and seed
concentration allowed for varying nanoparticle volumes while
keeping the LSPR’s position. From a broader perspective, the
expanded synthesis space presented here opens up the possi-
bilities for further evaluation of other experimental parameters
(e.g., pH[71]) to ultimately consolidate AuBPs in a wide range of
applications.
4. Experimental Section

Synthesis of Gold Seeds:
The gold seeds were prepared by fast reduc-
tion of gold precursor with NaBH4 in the presence of a cationic surfactant
(CTAC) and citric acid in a 20 mL scintillation vial (see Video S1, Sup-
porting Information). To an aqueous solution of CTAC (10 mL, 50 mM)
was added a solution of HAuCl4 (0.05 mL, 50 mM) followed by stirring
for ≈3 min until complexation of gold precursor with surfactant (trans-
parent, yellowish solution). Next, citric acid (0.05 mL, 1 m) was added
followed by the injection of freshly prepared NaBH4 (0.25 mL, 25 mM)
under vigorous stirring at 20 °C. The solution turned from yellow to
brownish immediately. 2 min later, the seed solution was placed in a sil-
icone oil bath and heated at 80 °C for 90 min under stirring. The solu-
tion color turned gradually from brown to red, indicating an increase in

tion of gold 0.25 mM) was removed from the oil bath, stored at room tem-
perature, and used without further treatment (see Video S2, Supporting
Information).

Synthesis of Gold Bipyramids:
To prepare the growth solution, an indi-
cated amount of CTAB was dissolved in an aqueous CTAC solution (20 mL,
100 mM) in a water bath at 35 °C. The mixture was kept under stirring at
35 °C for 10 min. After dissolution of the binary surfactant mixture, HAuCl4
solution (0.2 mL, 25 mM) was added and the solution was stirred at 35 °C
for 5 min to obtain a transparent yellowish solution. Subsequently, AgNO3
(0.06 mL, 10 mM) and 8-HQL (0.2 mL, 0.4 m in ethanol) were added and
the color of the growth solution changed from yellowish to colorless. After
30 s, a desired amount of gold seed solution was added to the growth so-
lution under vigorous stirring. After 15 min, an aliquot of 8-HQL (0.15 mL,
0.4 m in ethanol) was added dropwise, and ﬁnally, the mixture was kept at
the indicated time in a water bath at 35 °C under stirring (see details in
Tables S1–S6 and Video S3, Supporting Information, and Video S4, Sup-
porting Information). Finally, the gold bipyramids dispersions were cen-
trifuged twice (under the conditions as indicated in Supporting Informa-
tion) to remove the excess of reagents and redispersed in water.

Overgrowth of Gold Bipyramids:
To overgrowth gold bipyramids, the
same growth solution was used in the formation of gold bipyramids from
gold seeds (see details in Table S7, Supporting Information). A dispersion
of gold bipyramids with 66 nm in length and, 19 nm in width were used
as seeds, with a metallic gold concentration of 5 mM in CTAC 10 mM. Fi-
nally, the overgrown gold bipyramids dispersions were centrifuged twice
(6000 rpm, 3900 RCF, 30 min) to remove the excess reagents and redis-
persed in water.

The materials, information on sample analysis and analysis as well as
further characterization are provided in Supporting Information.

Statistical Analysis:
The data related to the nanoparticles dimensions
(length and width) were presented as the mean values, and error bars indi-

cate the standard error of the mean. The sample size for statistical analysis
was over 200.
